claim: Single-word metaphoric framing (crime as beast vs virus) shifted free-text solutions by about 17-18 points in the original lab (74% vs 56%, 71% vs 54%), and by about 10-11 points in forced-choice follow-ups (42% vs 31%, N=939). The shift is toward the frame's implied action. Later same-lab and related work gives smaller effects: w=.09-.16 (d01); antagonist-metaphor severity judgements d=.15-.20 once well powered (d02).
agent_test: Give the agent one problem with two competing source-domain framings in the first sentence; count how often the final plan type flips. Equal tokens; compare to a neutral 'problem' framing.

claim: An independent four-experiment replication (N=253, 259, 252, 1,026; Dutch and US) with a neutral control and a pre-exposure baseline found no beast/virus framing effect (all p>=.34), so the human framing effect is not robust across designs. Same-lab reanalysis (d01) says the null came from a shifted 'neighborhood watch' option; recoded, Steen Exp 4 gives chi2(4)=8.61, p=.072 and the pooled N=876 gives p=.003, w=.14. No independent preregistered replication was found.
agent_test: Treat the human framing effect size as unreliable; never assume a reframe helps. Always measure against a no-reframe arm.

claim: Metaphor framing worked only when placed first: the same metaphor at the end of the report had no effect (69% vs 64%, p=.59) versus 40% vs 22% when first.
agent_test: Test the reframe placed before vs after the facts at equal tokens. Same lab only, so keep as a hypothesis.

claim: The effect needs an integrated frame, not a keyword: a lexical prime of beast or virus without the metaphor gave no difference (64% vs 65%, p=.99). Evidence a15 misstates these Exp 3 numbers; b02 and the PLOS paper are correct.
agent_test: Compare a full correspondence table vs a single cue word in the prompt.

claim: People rarely name the metaphor as influential (3-15% across experiments), and recalling it did not change the effect (54% vs 56% congruent). Self-report of influence is not a valid check.
agent_test: Check whether the model's own rationale mentions the frame when its answer shifts; expect a low mention rate.

claim: Across 91 studies (N=34,783) metaphor frames beat literal frames by only d=0.11, with concept-level frames (d=0.22, k=36) far stronger than word-level frames (d=0.04, k=55), and science/education topics weaker (d=0.11). Small-study effects were present.
agent_test: Expect small, topic-dependent gains. Measure O6 gain by task type; prefer a full structural mapping over one analogy word.

claim: Embodied-metaphor priming effects replicate poorly: warmth and prosocial choice (original OR=3.52, N=50; pooled replication OR=0.77, N=861; Chabris N=128 and 177, r near 0) and head-heart moral judgement (N=203 and 304) all null.
agent_test: Do not borrow human effect sizes from embodied priming. Do not design the agent on the premise that bodily grounding matters.

claim: Positive-is-UP congruency effects are better explained by polarity correspondence than by an automatic GOOD IS UP mapping (effect vanished when 75% of words were negative, N=68).
agent_test: Mapping effects can be stimulus artifacts; balance polarity of labels in source and target in any agent test.

claim: The space-to-time mapping has the best behavioural support: primed frames shifted answers on the move-forward-two-days question (71.3%), space primes time more than time primes space, and line-length effects are asymmetric. The mapping varies across languages (Aymara, Mandarin, Spain vs Morocco).
agent_test: Source must be concrete and the direction concrete to abstract. Test mapping an ordering or time task into a spatial layout vs plain text at equal tokens. Original papers were read only via a review chapter.

claim: Cross-domain priming has a processing cost: ERP congruity effects were smaller for metaphorical time sentences than literal space sentences (N=24 and N=12), and time did not prime space.
agent_test: Count mapping overhead in tokens; check that the gain exceeds the cost at equal budget.

claim: Frontier LLMs interpret familiar metaphors at near-human accuracy: GPT-4 91.27% vs humans 94.42% on Fig-QA (1,146 items), GPT-3 Davinci 68.41%, fine-tuned RoBERTa 90.32%; accuracy rises with model size.
agent_test: The understand-the-metaphor step is not the bottleneck for strong models; spend tokens on applying the mapping.

claim: GPT-4 interprets novel literary metaphors at or above student level (blind ratings, source effect p=.045) and restores the canonical meaning of reversed metaphors at 56% vs 50% for humans (r=.79 over 55 items).
agent_test: One lab; translated Serbian poems may leak into training data. Use freshly written metaphors.

claim: Older and smaller LLMs fail when metaphor is cast as a cross-domain mapping: MUNCH paraphrase judgement mostly at or below the 0.25 chance level for LLaMA-13B, LLaMA-30B and GPT-3.5; generation MRR .33, .47, .54. Evidence c08 mislabels model order; Table 3 of the paper gives 13B .33, 30B .47, GPT-3.5 .54. Newer models do not fix it: GPT-4, GPT-4o, o3-mini and R1 still give concept-irrelevant readings in 15-25% of outputs (d06), and open 7B-72B models score higher on metaphors than on literal paraphrases because of lexical overlap (d05).
agent_test: Rerun MUNCH-style apt vs inapt judgement on the current model to see if literal-source distractors still fool it.

claim: GPT-3 naming of the source domain is unreliable on realistic text: 81.33% on a curated list, 53.74% on English LCC, 34.65% on Spanish LCC; most errors were invented source domains.
agent_test: When the agent picks its own source domain, have code check that each source element maps to a stated target element; expect invented mappings. Not re-verified in this pass.

claim: Metaphoricity is encoded in the middle layers of BERT, RoBERTa and ELECTRA and transfers across four languages, but detecting a metaphor is not using a mapping; probe gaps over baseline are small on some sets (TroFi about 68 vs 67).
agent_test: No direct agent test; relevant only to model-internal explanations.

claim: Mapping-conditioned generation works: CM-BART beats unconditioned generators on source-domain evocation (2.87 vs 2.12 for MERMAID; exact match 29.3% vs 13.3%), but annotator agreement was only .37-.50 and the per-cell table is partly scrambled in the PDF text.
agent_test: Supplying explicit source and target domains steers output. Test an explicit correspondence list vs a free restatement.

claim: Metaphor-style instructions can mislead code models: metaphorical wording raised inefficient-algorithm choice from 9.6% to 23.3% (Qwen), 4.4% to 34.5% (DeepSeek), 2.9% to 23.6% (Gemma) per sample. A second paper (Hu et al. 2026, arXiv 2601.03388) finds in-context danger metaphors raised critical misaligned answers from 20% to 40% in Qwen3-32B.
agent_test: A source-domain restatement can import a wrong procedure. Test: after restating, drop source inferences that conflict with target facts (invariance check) and compare error rate. One paper, not re-verified.

claim: Published metaphor-prompting for LLMs has weak evidence: one 100-problem self-built benchmark, four small models, LLM judge, bar charts only. Reread in the gap pass: the text has no numeric tables, variance or significance tests.
agent_test: Do not cite as support for O6; run our own comparison at equal tokens.

claim: Chain-of-thought rationales built from metaphor theory help weak GPT-3 Curie (2.49 to 2.76; QUD vs no-rationale not significant, beta=.41 [-.02,.84]) and do not help strong DaVinci (3.71 to 3.74).
agent_test: Structured reasoning scaffolds help weaker models more than strong ones. Compare scaffold vs plain across model sizes.

claim: Same-domain analogy and abstraction prompts help LLM reasoning: Step-Back lifts PaLM-2L MMLU Physics 66.4 to 73.2 (GPT-4 69.4 to 84.5 but CoT alone 82.9), self-generated analogs lift GSM8K 75.0 to 77.8, thought propagation +12 to +15 points. These are not cross-domain metaphors.
agent_test: Nearest tested analogues of O6; compare metaphor restatement directly with step-back and self-generated analogs at equal tokens.

claim: LLM analogy is brittle outside familiar forms: GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 fall to 0.35-0.49 on counterfactual letter-string alphabets vs humans 0.753; SCAN metaphor mappings gave MRR .022 (GPT-2) and .048 (BERT).
agent_test: Test the mapping on an unfamiliar source domain; a familiar source is safer. SCAN models are old and small.

claim: GPT-3 matched or beat students on analogical reasoning tasks (digit matrices OR=1.88, letter strings OR=1.76), though the same models are brittle on counterfactual variants.
agent_test: Compare on transfer analogy tests with novel domains; the result depends on test familiarity.

claim: Metaphor-based black-white IAT bias is as strong as the race IAT (d=1.44 vs 1.12, N=200), suggesting conceptual metaphors can carry value bias into judgement. IAT validity is itself disputed.
agent_test: A value-loaded source domain (good/evil) may import bias into target judgement; test neutral vs loaded sources.

claim: Metaphor framing beats literal framing only by small amounts on reasoning and risk judgement, and nulls exist. Antagonist-metaphor disaster framing: d=.47 (Study 1, N=363) falling to d=.15 (N=636) and d=.20 (N=937). Vaccine extended metaphors vs literal: no difference in attitude gain (interaction F=0.059, p=.81, N=301).
agent_test: Always include a literal-restatement arm. Expect effect sizes near d=.15-.20, not the .5 of early studies.

claim: The beast/virus effect depends on how answer options are scored. Re-scoring one option ('neighborhood watch') with 2014 norms moved it from enforcement-leaning to reform-leaning and changed the Steen Exp 4 result from clearly null to chi2 p=.072.
agent_test: Pre-register the scoring of each answer type before testing a reframe on the agent; a post hoc recode can create or hide a result.

claim: Logically equivalent framings change LLM choices a lot. In 82 models from 11 families, a survival-vs-collective framing moved P(B) from 4.3% to 68.8% (64.5 points). DeepSeek was the least sensitive family (shift .10, p=.319). Reasoning traces lowered B rates in an exploratory check (.811 to .254).
agent_test: Test the final answer for flip under an equivalent reframe. A frame-invariance check is a cheap guard.

claim: A restate-in-opposite-frame prompt reduces framing bias in small LLMs: DeFrame cut framing disparity by an average 92% and bias score by 93% on BBQ (8 models, 3B-14B, four calls per question).
agent_test: Implement: restate problem in two frames, answer both, reconcile. Compare to one frame at equal calls.

claim: Same-domain restatement is the best-supported cousin of O6. Rephrase and Respond lifted GPT-4 average accuracy from 64.95 to 89.77 over ten tasks (2023). No study restates into a different source domain at equal tokens against RaR, step-back and CoT.
agent_test: Use RaR as the primary baseline for any source-domain restatement test; count tokens.

claim: A spatial restatement helps on spatial tasks only. Visualization-of-Thought raised GPT-4 route-planning success from 9.48 to 14.72 and next-step accuracy from 54.00 to 59.00; it helped LLaMA3-70B but not LLaMA3-8B, and lost to CoT on ring navigation (49.5 vs 52.5).
agent_test: Use spatial restatement only when the task has an ordering or layout; do not assume it transfers to abstract tasks.

claim: LLM metaphor competence is partly surface cue use. Seven open models score 85-95% on metaphor sets but lower on literal paraphrases (Qwen2.5-72B CoT Figurative-NLI 95.43 vs 88.58); frontier and reasoning models still produce concept-irrelevant readings in 15-25% of outputs and gain from POS shuffling (R1 28.68 to 46.41).
agent_test: Add a check that each inference taken from the source domain is true of the target before it enters the plan (Invariance Principle check).

claim: LLMs over-detect metaphor: GPT-3.5 literal recall 5.59%, GPT-4-turbo 60.53%, GPT-4o 54.24% on TroFi (3,736 sentences). They are weak on prepositions and multi-word units.
agent_test: When asking the agent for the source domain, require a stated target fact the mapping explains, to cut spurious mappings.

claim: Value-loaded metaphors steer reasoning models: in Qwen3-32B, in-context danger metaphors doubled critical misaligned answers (20% to 40%) and concrete metaphors halved them (40% to 20%); poetry pre-training raised legal misalignment 23.8% to 60.4%.
agent_test: Strip evaluative words from the restated source domain; compare with a neutral-source arm.
